## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
\begin{marginfigure}
\resizebox{0.92\linewidth}{!}{\mlphysicalstackfull{20}{20}{20}{20}{100}}
\end{marginfigure}
:::

_Why can a large archive of successful demonstrations leave a robot unable to recover from its first mistake?_

A successful demonstration shows how one machine completed a task under one set of conditions. It shows almost nothing about what to do after a slip, a shifted fixture, or a worn gripper, yet a learned policy's first error carries it into exactly those states, where the archive holds no instruction. Repeating the demonstration enlarges the archive without filling that gap. The recorded motion also carries the operator's delay, the machine's limits, and every correction the permission path applied, so a training process that cannot separate these influences learns a safeguard's intervention or a mechanical limitation as if it were skill. Gathering the missing experience costs operator time and component life, and the collection itself must stay within the machine's physical limits. Physical data must therefore be engineered, from the choice of experiences to the meaning, timing, and physical origin of every label and the conditions the archive leaves uncovered. Because every collected action crosses the causal boundary, its irreversible costs decide what a machine can learn and where its evidence stops.

{{< pagebreak >}}

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Analyze the conditional quadratic imitation-cost bound and distinguish dataset occupancy from evaluated closed-loop competence
- Select the action tap a dataset imitates and align multi-rate sensor and action streams to hardware exposure-midpoint timestamps within the task's spatial tolerance
- Estimate usable demonstration yield from collection time, operator rest, and physical reset overhead, and budget the mechanical component wear a campaign consumes
- Identify collection gaps by joining empirical state-action occupancy against a required scenario ledger
- Separate failed autonomous actions from admissible human recovery across the divergence, takeover, and stabilization timestamps in authority-record entries
- Evaluate whether an embodiment's mechanical, sensing, and timing assumptions transfer to another machine without falling into the normalization fallacy
- Detect silent calibration and plant drift in a demonstration archive using kinematic reprojection and repeated excitation trajectories
- Design an immutable demonstration provenance record linking each observation to its four-stream action taps ($a_{\text{req}}, a_{\text{cmd}}, a_{\text{enf}}, a_{\text{meas}}$) and to the collecting plant

:::

## Endogenous Experience {#sec-data-endogenous-experience}

In most machine learning, the dataset exists before the engineering begins. A text corpus or an image benchmark is gathered independently of the model, costs little per additional example, and does not change in response to anything the model predicts. A physical machine has no such corpus. Its training data is manufactured by running the machine, so every demonstration consumes operator time and component life. Each record also reflects who chose the actions, what the permission path admitted, and what the body actually did, and each executed action changes the states that later observations can show. Physical data is therefore an engineered artifact. The central question of physical data engineering is which experience to collect, and what to record about it, so that a policy learns the task rather than the circumstances of its collection. Answering it requires four things: a price for collection in operator time and wear, a precise meaning for every action label, a measure of coverage that does not depend on the archive's own contents, and a record that states what the archive leaves out.

The warehouse mobile manipulator can enforce its motion limits and still lack the experience needed to open its spring-latched cage door. During a demonstration, an operator requests motion, the permission path checks it, and the body moves against the latch. The sensor log records the outcome of that entire loop. The limit records and the handoff record established by the machine's anatomy therefore become conditions on the data used to teach its learned proposer. Choosing what experience to collect requires understanding how actions change subsequent observations; choosing what to imitate requires separating the requested action from the permitted command and measured response.

A policy trained on the retained demonstrations of a door-opening campaign, clean teleoperated openings of the warehouse mobile manipulator's spring-latched cage door, can still fail at the latch on its first autonomous attempt. One cause is the shift the machine's own actions create. Unlike a prediction on a fixed dataset, an executed action in an embodied Markov Decision Process (MDP), a task model in which the next state depends only on the current state and action (@sec-training-rl-primer), changes the body's physical trajectory, camera pose, and contact states, thereby altering the distribution of all subsequent observations ($s_{t+1} \sim P(s \mid s_t, a_t)$).

::: {#dfn-data-endogenous-covariate-shift .callout-definition title="Endogenous covariate shift"}

***Endogenous covariate shift***\index{Endogenous covariate shift!definition}\index{Covariate drift!physical AI} is the closed-loop distribution discrepancy wherein an embodied agent's executed actions alter its subsequent physical states and sensory observations ($s_{t+1} \sim P(s \mid s_t, a_t)$), driving the system into state-space regimes unsupported by its training demonstrations.

1.  **Significance**: Explains how offline behavioral cloning can fail during closed-loop physical execution: a perturbation may drive the system into states where the policy lacks training support.
2.  **Distinction**: Unlike exogenous dataset shift caused by changing ambient lighting or seasonal weather, endogenous shift is actively generated by the agent's own closed-loop actions altering its subsequent observation distribution.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Attempting to fix closed-loop policy failure by collecting more nominal expert demonstrations, which only increases data density along the success manifold without providing the corrective recovery data needed to escape boundary excursions.

:::

This shift is the collection-side face of principle \ref{pri-vol4-endogenous-drift}. It makes an archive of flawless executions without recovery trajectories an operational liability, because the policy's first mistake moves the robot outside the demonstrated states.

### Mechanics of endogenous covariate shift {#sec-data-covariate-shift}

In classical statistical learning theory, empirical risk minimization assumes that samples are drawn independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) from an exogenous, stationary distribution $\mathcal{D}$. An image classifier that misidentifies a dog as a cat does not alter the pixels of subsequent images in the test set. The covariate shift of imitation learning, introduced in @sec-boundary-causal-boundary, is the closed-loop, endogenous case defined above. Passive machine learning uses the same name for an open-loop observational phenomenon, the contrast case here: the marginal input distribution $P(X)$ changes (such as evaluating a vision model trained on sunny daytime driving under rainy nighttime illumination) while the underlying conditional data-generating function $P(Y \mid X)$ remains stationary. The model is a passive observer: its predictions $\hat{Y}$ exert zero physical back-action on the data source, and an inference error does not physically mutate subsequent inputs.

In a physical machine, two distinct mechanisms can change what the learner encounters. The first changes which states the policy visits even when the plant is unchanged; the second changes how the plant responds to an action:

1. **Endogenous state distribution shift**: The policy's executed actions $\mathbf{a}_t = \pi_\theta(\mathbf{o}_t)$ directly alter the state transition $\mathbf{s}_{t+1} \sim P(\mathbf{s} \mid \mathbf{s}_t, \mathbf{a}_t)$, actively shaping what sensory observations $\mathbf{o}_{t+1}$ the machine encounters next. An execution error displaces the physical body into an unvisited state, immediately mutating the input distribution.
2. **Active physical plant drift**: The governing physical plant is a continuous dynamical system whose differential equations of motion $\dot{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{u}; \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{plant}}(t))$ actively drift over operational time. Actuator Joule heating ($I^2 R$) raises winding temperature and copper resistance $R(T) = R_0(1 + \alpha \Delta T)$, which reduces the drive's voltage headroom and therefore the current, and torque, it can deliver at speed; cyclic loading of strain-wave gears degrades lubrication, lowers torsional stiffness, and increases lost motion; compliant elastomer gripper pads abrade and deform, shrinking the Coulomb friction cone ($\|\mathbf{F}_t\| \le \mu F_n$); and manipulated workpieces exhibit unmodeled variations in mass, center of gravity, and surface roughness across trials, altering the inertia the arm must accelerate and the gravity load it must hold.

In embodied control, the policy's actions induce an *endogenous state visitation distribution* $d^\pi(s)$, the fraction of time steps at which a rollout of policy $\pi$ occupies state $s$. When a policy trains via offline behavioral cloning on demonstrations generated by an expert policy $\pi^*$, it minimizes imitation loss over the expert's occupancy distribution $d^{\pi^*}(s)$. During autonomous execution, however, the policy must generate actions under its own induced distribution $d^\pi(s)$. The divergence between $d^{\pi^*}$ and $d^\pi$ can compound errors when the learned policy lacks a recovery action.

::: {#dfn-data-behavioral-cloning .callout-definition title="Behavioral cloning"}

***Behavioral cloning***\index{Behavioral cloning!definition} is imitation learning posed as supervised learning: a policy is fit to map each recorded observation to the action the demonstrator took there, with the loss weighted by the demonstrator's own state occupancy $d^{\pi^*}$.

1.  **Significance**: Training error is measured only on states the demonstrator visited, while deployment cost accrues on the states the learned policy visits. Under a 0–1 action loss the worst-case excess cost can therefore grow with the square of the horizon $T$ rather than linearly, as the next subsection derives.
2.  **Distinction**: Unlike corrective aggregation, which obtains expert labels at states the learner itself reaches, behavioral cloning never observes the consequences of its own mistakes; unlike reinforcement learning, it needs demonstrations but no reward.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Reading a low held-out loss as evidence of closed-loop competence. A held-out split drawn from the same demonstrations shares their occupancy, so it cannot contain the states the policy's first error reaches.

:::

### Recovery and compounding error {#sec-data-curse-dimensionality-recoverability}

Opening the latch from a centered approach and recovering from a sideways slip require different actions. @Fig-05-latch-corridor shows the approach from above. Every retained demonstration moves the gripper forward along a narrow corridor centered on the strike plate, so the archive holds thousands of forward-progress actions. It holds no action that starts from a gripper displaced a few millimeters toward the fixture and returns it to the centerline, because a skilled operator rarely lets the gripper drift there, and a run that did drift was usually stopped or discarded.[^fn-alvinn-recovery-latch] At such a displaced state no demonstration constrains the policy's output. The **recoverability problem**\index{Recoverability problem} is this missing instruction for returning to the corridor.

[^fn-alvinn-recovery-latch]: **ALVINN (Autonomous Land Vehicle in a Neural Network)**\index{ALVINN!recovery data}: Pomerleau's road-following network learned to steer from a human driver who kept the van centered, so its training images held almost no off-center views [@pomerleau1989alvinn]. His remedy shifted each camera image sideways in software and corrected the steering label to match, synthesizing recovery examples about 20 years before DAgger [@pomerleau1991efficient]. A warp could fill that gap because the missing state was only a viewpoint of a flat road, whereas a gripper displaced toward the fixture also lacks contact forces that no image transform can manufacture, so its recoveries must be demonstrated or collected.

::: {#fig-05-latch-corridor fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**The latch corridor seen from above**: Retained demonstrations supply dense forward-progress actions inside a narrow corridor centered on the strike plate. A gripper displaced toward the fixture sits where the archive holds no demonstration, so nothing in the data specifies the action that returns it to the corridor, and an unconstrained output can carry it farther toward contact." fig-alt="Top-view sketch. A shaded horizontal corridor runs left to right toward a strike plate on the right, with five arrows pointing along its centerline. Above the corridor, a small square marks a displaced gripper. A dashed arrow from the gripper toward the corridor is labeled as the missing return action, and a dashed arrow from the gripper toward a shaded fixture band at the top is labeled as drift into contact."}
![](images/svg/fig05_latch_corridor.svg){width="100%"}
:::

Whether the missing return action matters depends on the closed loop. The robot's state includes joint coordinates, velocities, drive currents, contact wrenches (the combined contact forces and torques), and camera images, so a nominal demonstration samples only a thin path through a high-dimensional space, and most small displacements lead off that path. If the plant and its low-level controllers pull a small lateral error back toward the centerline on their own, an imperfect policy output near the corridor still lets the error decay. If they do not, the error persists or grows until a recovery action, the permission path, or a human intervenes. Actual archives do include some corrections, and their support must be measured against the scenario ledger rather than assumed (@sec-data-policy-coverage).

We can see the quadratic worst-case scaling through basic discrete summation. Consider a possible first error at step $t \in \{1, \dots, T\}$, before which the agent has followed the expert trajectory. If the deviation reaches an unsupported state and the agent never recovers, the remaining horizon can incur a penalty at every step ($T - t$). Assigning each possible error time the same upper probability contribution $\epsilon$ and a normalized unit cost ($c_t = 1$) gives the following accumulation. It illustrates an upper-bound argument, not an exact expectation over independent first-error events:
$$\sum_{t=1}^T \epsilon (T - t) = \epsilon \left( T^2 - \sum_{t=1}^T t \right) = \epsilon \left( T^2 - \frac{T(T+1)}{2} \right) = \frac{T(T-1)}{2} \epsilon \approx \frac{1}{2} T^2 \epsilon.$$
Contrast this result with open-loop supervised prediction: if errors at each step were independent and did not alter future inputs, an $\epsilon$ per-step error rate would accumulate linearly over $T$ steps as $\sum_{t=1}^T \epsilon = T\epsilon$. The extra factor of $T$ in $\mathcal{O}(T^2\epsilon)$ is the mathematical signature of closed-loop endogenous feedback.

The quadratic term describes accumulated task cost, not a trajectory. It does not say that position error grows as $t^2$. Feedback, contact, and saturation shape how a physical deviation evolves; the argument concerns only the cost of time spent in states where the policy lacks a demonstrated correction.

Formally, let $\pi$ be the learned policy, $\pi^*$ the expert, $J$ expected cumulative task cost over $T$ steps, and $\epsilon$ the probability of disagreement on expert-visited states under 0–1 action loss: $\mathbb{E}_{s \sim d^{\pi^*}} [\mathbb{I}(\pi(s) \ne \pi^*(s))] \le \epsilon$. If per-step task cost lies in $[0,1]$, behavioral cloning\index{Behavioral cloning!quadratic error compounding} admits the worst-case bound (@eq-data-quadratic-drift) derived by @ross2010efficient and restated by @ross2011reduction:
$$J(\pi)-J(\pi^*) \le T^2\epsilon.$$ {#eq-data-quadratic-drift}

The bound can exceed the total cost available in a finite episode. With nonnegative per-step cost at most one, the excess cost is also bounded by $T$, so $\min(T, T^2\epsilon)$ is the useful upper bound. Once the quadratic expression exceeds $T$, it supplies no tighter prediction of failure frequency or physical severity. Its engineering value is to expose the missing recovery assumption, not to predict that every small error causes a collision. @Sec-appendix-ml-compounding derives the bound and states its loss and bounded-cost assumptions.

Which horizon dependence applies depends on the loss, the action space, and the closed loop, so @eq-data-quadratic-drift is best read as the classical result for a 0–1 action loss rather than as a law of behavioral cloning. Trained with the logarithmic loss (the negative log-probability the learned policy assigns to the expert's action) on a policy class that contains the expert, behavioral cloning can reach a sample complexity, the number of demonstrations needed for a given excess cost, that does not grow with the horizon, provided cumulative reward is bounded and the policy class is not too rich [@foster2024behavior]. Continuous actions push the other way. Even when the closed loop is exponentially stable, so that the effect of a small perturbation decays at a fixed exponential rate, and the expert is smooth and deterministic, any smooth deterministic imitator can suffer execution error exponentially larger in the horizon than its error on the expert's own states. The escapes are policies that are non-smooth, non-Markovian, or strongly state-dependent in their randomness, as action-chunking and diffusion decoders are, or demonstrations spread widely enough around the expert's path [@simchowitz2025pitfalls]. The latch policy acts in a continuous space, so the question the corridor sketch poses, whether the closed loop pulls a displaced gripper back, is the one on which the modern theory turns.

Recording more nominal expert demonstrations does not resolve endogenous covariate shift. Another thousand hours of clean, centered openings increases sample density along the nominal trajectory, but the empirical support outside the nominal tube remains zero ($d^{\pi^*}(s) = 0$). This is the *nominal demonstration trap*. Gathering physical experience also has a physical price. A web crawler ingests static text with no marginal hardware depreciation, whereas every recorded second of physical robotics telemetry consumes actuator fatigue life, heats motor windings ($dT/dt$), cycles gearbox teeth, and drains the battery. In the illustrative campaign below, operator rest, calibration, scene resets, and rejected trials leave less than one quarter of scheduled cell time as retained demonstration data (@sec-data-teleop-costs). Physical demonstration data is scarce and expensive; logging it without accounting for closed-loop dynamics misleads policy training.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Actuator thermal dissipation ($dT/dt$) and winding damage limits are derived in @sec-body-thermal-duty-cycles.
:::

A physical command also changes meaning on its way to the actuators. In a machine divided by the proposal boundary (@sec-boundary-machine-model), the operator's or policy's request is mapped into a setpoint, admitted or modified by the permission path, and answered by the plant with a measured response. Logging only the request trains the policy on demands the plant could never execute, and logging only the response teaches it structural deflection and gear backlash as though they were deliberate human skill.

A collection campaign therefore makes two decisions before it records anything: which source will choose the actions, and which of those four forms of each action the dataset will keep as its label.

## Physical Telemetry Sources and Ingestion Modalities {#sec-data-collection-sources}

For the cage-door latch, an operator can guide the arm directly, command it through a remote interface, or let a controller choose the next motion. Each choice changes which errors and corrections reach the archive. Physical collection also consumes plant time and wear, so choosing a source is a decision about useful experience per attempted episode.

In a streaming telemetry architecture, physical data sources separate according to who chooses the action and how the control stream enters the ingestion pipeline:

1. In **kinesthetic teaching**, a colocated human demonstrator physically grasps and guides the unpowered or gravity-compensated links of the mechanism. The pipeline logs joint encoder positions at the controller rate without teleoperation transport latency, but the demonstrated motion's bandwidth is set by the human arm, which moves far more slowly than the controller samples, and labor cost scales $1:1$ with demonstrator time. The demonstrator's body also occludes camera fields of view, altering the visual distribution compared to autonomous operation.
2. In **teleoperation**, a remote operator manipulates an input device to puppet the follower robot across a network fabric.[^fn-goertz-force-teleop] Interfaces differ in how the operator's motion maps to the robot and in what contact information returns to the operator. Joint-space leader-follower arms such as ALOHA [@zhao2023learning] and GELLO [@wu2023gello] share the follower's joint topology, usually at reduced scale, so leader joint angles copy to the follower without inverse kinematics (computing the joint angles that place the tool at a commanded pose, @sec-appendix-control-kinematics); tracked spatial controllers and rate-controlled space mice command tool poses or velocities through inverse kinematics; and force-reflecting bilateral arms return measured contact force to the operator's hands. @Tbl-05-teleop-taxonomy compares these interfaces and names the artifact each leaves in the recording.
3. In **scripted collection**, a deterministic trajectory generator executes automated motion primitives, such as cubic splines or impedance-governed state machines. Ingestion rates are high and deterministic ($50\text{--}500\text{ Hz}$), but trajectories follow rigid, repetitive manifolds that fail to generate corrective data for off-nominal contacts, jamming when workpiece dimensions deviate by even a millimeter.
4. In **exploratory collection**, an active neural policy or reinforcement learning agent selects actions to maximize an information-theoretic objective (such as epistemic entropy or intrinsic curiosity). While data throughput matches the robot's maximum control cadence ($50\text{--}100\text{ Hz}$), unbounded exploratory commands risk high-energy collisions, tripping safety enforcers or damaging mechanical gearboxes through repeated high-torque shock loads.
5. In **autonomous deployment logging**, production policies control the actuators during factory or warehouse operation, streaming multimodal telemetry into local circular buffers in situ. This stream provides zero-marginal-labor data at the full system execution rate ($10\text{--}50\text{ Hz}$ policy, $1\text{ kHz}$ joint servos), but logged states are heavily censored by runtime safety barriers and reflect only nominal operating regimes.
6. In **robot-free demonstration**, the operator carries a hand-held gripper fitted with a wrist camera and performs the task directly in the environment, as in the Universal Manipulation Interface [@chi2024umi]. Collection consumes neither robot time nor actuator life, and one device can gather data where no robot is installed. The cost moves to the labels. The device records its own trajectory and camera view but no robot's joint commands, so the action must be expressed relative to the gripper's pose and later executed through the target robot's own controller, and the deployed robot's observation and actuation latencies must be matched to the recording (@sec-data-multimodal-time-sync).

[^fn-goertz-force-teleop]: **Bilateral Telemanipulation**\index{Raymond Goertz!bilateral telemanipulation}: Raymond Goertz's 1949 master-slave manipulator at Argonne National Laboratory moved tongs behind radiation shielding in exact correspondence with a master handle, and its mechanical linkage returned the forces at the tongs to the operator's hand [@goertz1949master; @hokayem2006bilateral]. Remote manipulation therefore began with contact force inside the loop. A demonstration recorded through an interface that drops that force channel cannot contain the contact corrections the operator would have made by feel.

A seventh source removes the robot entirely. Simulation pipelines avoid hardware wear but replace the physical plant with a numerical model, and simulation now supplies demonstrations in its own right. A generator can adapt a few hundred human demonstrations to new object poses and scene layouts and replay them in simulation to produce tens of thousands more [@mandlekar2023mimicgen], and a policy can be co-trained on simulated and real data at a declared mixing ratio. Such records must identify their source, generator, engine version, and contact parameters, and the scenario ledger must mark any cell that only synthetic experience fills, so that training and diagnosis can distinguish simulator artifacts from measured plant behavior. The provenance those records need is set out under dataset degradation (@sec-data-sim-to-real-artifacts), while @sec-training examines the contact approximations and their consequences for learning.

Because the source determines how the machine interacts with its physical environment, these ingestion streams occupy disjoint state-action manifolds even when executing the identical manipulation task. Consider releasing the warehouse mobile manipulator's cage-door latch. A colocated demonstrator guiding the arm feels the latch bind through direct tactile resistance and immediately modulates wrist compliance. A remote teleoperator watching compressed video streams lacks direct tactile feedback and exhibits step-and-wait hunting, pausing to visually verify strike plate contact. A scripted controller advances along a fixed geometric path at constant velocity, producing an identical, rigid contact force spike on every repetition. An exploratory policy approaches at oblique angles, binding the latch until the safety contact tripwire halts the attempt. These recorded streams are not noisy variations of a single ground-truth trajectory; they are outputs of distinct dynamical systems characterized by divergent bandwidths, latencies, and mechanical compliance profiles, as systematized in @tbl-05-sources-taxonomy.

| Physical Data Source                     | Ingestion Bandwidth & Cadence                                                    | Contact Compliance & Force Awareness                     | Scaling Labor Economics                                     | ODD Boundary Safety Risk                                           |
|:-----------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Kinesthetic teaching**                 | Controller rate; motion bandwidth set by the human arm                           | High (direct physical feel of binding and compliance)    | Very high ($1:1$ dedicated human demonstrator)              | Low (demonstrator immediately feels binding forces)                |
| **Teleoperation (bilateral/isomorphic)** | Moderate ($20\text{--}50\text{ Hz}$, network + human latency)                    | Moderate to high (depends on haptic force feedback)      | High ($1:1$ human operator per active cell)                 | Low to moderate (guarded by operator situational awareness)        |
| **Scripted primitives**                  | High ($50\text{--}500\text{ Hz}$, deterministic trajectory generators)           | Low (rigid trajectories unless impedance-governed)       | Low (automated once authored; engineering upfront)          | High (blind trajectory replay jams on geometric misalignments)     |
| **Exploratory policy**                   | High ($50\text{--}100\text{ Hz}$, active neural exploration)                     | Variable (learned or randomized contact behaviors)       | Very low (fully autonomous hardware execution)              | Very high (unbounded exploratory actions risk destructive contact) |
| **Autonomous deployment logging**        | Full system rate ($10\text{--}50\text{ Hz}$ policy, $1\text{ kHz}$ joint servos) | Operational (reflects live deployed closed-loop control) | Zero marginal labor (harvested passively during production) | Guarded (governed by certified runtime safety enforcer)            |
| **Robot-free hand-held device**          | Device camera and pose rate; no robot joint stream                               | High (operator feels real contact through the device)    | Moderate (one person per device; no robot time or wear)     | None to the robot; labels need execution on a target robot         |
| **Synthetic generation**                 | Simulator step rate, limited by compute                                          | Modeled (contact set by engine and parameters)           | Low after seed demonstrations are recorded                  | None during collection; model artifacts surface at deployment      |

: **Systems trade-offs across physical demonstration and telemetry sources**: Seven collection sources compared across control dynamics, contact awareness, human labor economics, and physical safety risks during data capture. {#tbl-05-sources-taxonomy tbl-colwidths="[20,20,20,20,20]"}

```{python}
#| label: calc-data-effective-sample-size
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ EFFECTIVE SAMPLE SIZE OF CORRELATED TELEMETRY (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-data-collection-sources (effective sample size paragraph)
# │ Goal:    Show how few independent observations one hour of 1 kHz logging
# │          holds when adjacent records are almost perfectly correlated.
# │ Show:    Records per hour; lag-1 correlation; effective sample size.
# │ How:     N = rate * 1 h; N_eff = N (1 - rho) / (1 + rho) for an AR(1)
# │          statistic (Thiebaux and Zwiers 1984).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_int, fmt_sci, fmt_frequency, fmt_latency, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

class EffectiveSampleSize:
    """Effective sample size of one hour of permission-tick telemetry."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    f_log = RM.permission_rate  # one record per permission tick; category: datasheet
    t_log = 1.0 * hour  # category: chosen
    rho = 0.999  # lag-1 autocorrelation of a slowly varying statistic; category: illustrative

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    n_records = (f_log * t_log).to("").magnitude
    n_eff = n_records * (1.0 - rho) / (1.0 + rho)
    ratio = n_records / n_eff

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Assertions) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(n_records - 3.6e6) < 1e-6, "One hour at 1 kHz should be 3.6 million records")
    check(1790 < n_eff < 1810, "Effective sample size should be about 1,800")
    check(1000 < ratio < 10000, "Step count should overstate independent samples by three orders of magnitude")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    f_log_str = fmt_frequency(f_log, unit=ureg.kilohertz, precision=0)
    n_records_str = fmt_sci(n_records, precision=1)
    rho_str = fmt(rho, precision=3)
    n_eff_str = fmt_int(round(n_eff, -2))
    t_tick_str = fmt_latency((1 / f_log).to(millisecond), unit=millisecond, precision=0)
```

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
⇄ **Contrast:** The display and operator-response delay that paces a teleoperator's step-and-wait motion (@sec-data-teleop-costs) contrasts with the `{python} EffectiveSampleSize.t_tick_str` permission tick on which each command is checked (@sec-nervous-cadences).
:::

The cheapest sources in the table also produce the most records, which invites a mistake imported from disembodied machine learning, where empirical scaling laws correlate model performance with raw token count or pretraining sample volume ($N$). In physical telemetry, treating each logged control step as an independent sample is a category error. An edge logger running at `{python} EffectiveSampleSize.f_log_str` generates `{python} EffectiveSampleSize.n_records_str` state-action records per hour, but adjacent records exhibit near-total temporal autocorrelation ($\rho \to 1.0$). Two kinematic records sampled `{python} EffectiveSampleSize.t_tick_str` apart differ only by sub-millimeter displacements and sensor quantization noise. For a stationary scalar telemetry statistic with geometrically decaying autocorrelation $\rho_k = \rho^k$, as in an AR(1) model, the large-sample *effective sample size* (ESS)[^fn-ess-correlated-telemetry] for estimating its mean is:
$$N_{\text{eff}} = N \frac{1 - \rho}{1 + \rho}.$$ {#eq-data-effective-sample-size}
Under this model, $\rho =$ `{python} EffectiveSampleSize.rho_str` and `{python} EffectiveSampleSize.n_records_str` records give approximately `{python} EffectiveSampleSize.n_eff_str` effective observations for that statistic. Lag-1 correlation alone does not determine ESS for a general telemetry process, and ESS is not a count of covered task conditions. Unlike text tokens in large language models, where consecutive tokens represent high-entropy semantic transitions, consecutive high-frequency robot telemetry steps contain virtually zero new information about the task manifold. Autoregressive token volume does not equal physical state-space support. Dataset coverage scales with the number of independent physical episodes, workpiece initializations, lighting conditions, and surface friction coefficients, not with the sampling clock. An archive of a few hundred episodes spanning diverse geometric and mechanical initial conditions provides broader empirical support than millions of steps logged across repetitive passes over a single stationary fixture.

[^fn-ess-correlated-telemetry]: **Effective Sample Size**\index{Effective sample size!serially correlated telemetry}: The factor $(1-\rho)/(1+\rho)$ is the variance inflation of the mean of a first-order autoregressive series, the correction climatologists apply to serially correlated weather records before testing a trend [@thiebaux1984interpretation]. At the correlation used here it turns an hour of permission-tick records into about `{python} EffectiveSampleSize.n_eff_str` independent ones, so a step count overstates what a telemetry archive knows by three orders of magnitude before coverage is even considered.

### Human demonstration idiosyncrasies and mechanical artifacts {#sec-data-human-idiosyncrasies}

Teleoperation datasets do not capture pure, ideal control laws; they permanently record the physiological idiosyncrasies and biomechanical limitations of the human demonstrator:

- **Neuromuscular sub-movements and physiological tremor:** Human motor control is not a continuous, smooth spline. Neuromuscular execution operates via discrete motor unit recruitment bursts, producing intermittent corrections at $2\text{--}3\text{ Hz}$ superimposed with physiological tremor at $8\text{--}12\text{ Hz}$. When high-frequency behavioral cloning models train on raw joint velocities without low-pass filtering, the neural network learns to reproduce this neuromuscular tremor as high-frequency torque ripple, inducing rapid mechanical wear on robot gearboxes.
- **Visual latency and step-and-wait hunting:** When an operator guides a manipulator toward a contact fixture using 2D monitor displays, depth ambiguity and transport latency force the operator to adopt a *step-and-wait* control strategy: they advance the gripper a few millimeters, pause for $200\text{--}400\text{ ms}$ to visually verify contact on the video stream, and then resume motion. A policy trained on these raw pauses internalizes periodic velocity dropouts, causing the autonomous robot to stutter and freeze mid-trajectory during deployment.
- **Attentional narrowing and gaze-conditioned bias:** Human demonstrators focus visual attention narrowly on the active tool center point (TCP). Because the human's gaze does not monitor peripheral joints, elbow links often sweep close to tables or fixtures during demonstrations. A policy that imitates these demonstrations inherits elbow trajectories that flirt with the boundary of collision without possessing the demonstrator's implicit spatial awareness.

Each of these artifacts enters the archive looking like intended behavior. Source selection determines which experience enters the archive; the choice of action label determines what the policy learns to imitate from it.

## Action Label Selection and Supervisory Grounding {#sec-data-action-label}

By the time the gripper contacts the strike plate on the cage-door latch, the operator's input motion has transformed into four distinct numerical signals across the system hierarchy (@fig-05-action-taps). Which signal the ingestion pipeline designates as the supervisory target determines what behavioral dynamics the neural policy internalizes. The robot splits its computational architecture across two decoupled processing domains:

- The unprivileged **Linux application processor** executes perception pipelines, handles video frame ingestion, runs teleoperation input mapping, and computes the neural policy forward pass ($\pi_\theta(o_t)$).
- On the permission side of the causal proposal boundary (@sec-boundary-machine-model), a hard real-time **safety microcontroller (MCU)** runs the joint and permission checks at the chosen `{python} EffectiveSampleSize.f_log_str` cadence. Dedicated motor-drive logic closes the faster field-oriented current loop; its current samples are distinct from the telemetry retained at each permission tick.[^fn-capture-encoder-dma]

[^fn-capture-encoder-dma]: **Hardware Input Capture**\index{Input capture!DMA latching}: On real-time MCUs, a timer's input-capture unit latches encoder counts and current-shunt conversions at a hardware edge, and Direct Memory Access (DMA) moves them to memory without waiting on software. Sampling jitter stays at microseconds, so the denominator of a numerically differentiated velocity or acceleration carries no scheduling noise.

### The four-stream action tap tuple {#sec-data-four-stream-action-tap}

The four taps in @fig-05-action-taps locate the transformations between operator input and plant response. Preserving each stage lets the training pipeline select a target while retaining the evidence needed to explain interventions and tracking error.

::: {#fig-05-action-taps fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Four-stream action tap tuple**: Four places a command can be logged, from raw policy intent on the application processor through to measured plant response. Which tap a dataset records decides what the model learns to imitate. The four-tap decomposition is this book's construct; the teleoperation rigs it instruments follow @zhao2023learning and @wu2023gello." fig-alt="Block diagram. On the application processor, a policy or operator box feeds a kinematic mapping box; tap 1, a req, sits between them and tap 2, a cmd, sits after the mapping. A black-channel link with no shared memory crosses the dashed proposal boundary to the discrete safety MCU, which holds the permission path at a 1 kHz tick. Tap 3, a enf, sits after the permission path, which feeds the drives that close the current loops and apply the torque limit. The drives move the plant, joint encoders measure the motion over an interval, and tap 4, a meas, leaves the encoders. All four taps run down to a synchronized telemetry log stamped with hardware timestamps."}
![](images/svg/fig05_four_stream_action_taps.svg){width="100%"}
:::

As mapped across the proposal boundary in @fig-05-action-taps, logging divided between the unprivileged Linux host and the hard real-time MCU captures four distinct physical semantics:

- **Tap 1: The requested action ($a_{\text{req}}$, "Asked"):** Logged in user space on the application processor, this represents unconstrained human operator input (from a leader arm or joystick) or the raw forward-pass output from an unverified policy, tagged with its native coordinate frame and issue timestamp prior to software validation. This proposal reflects unadulterated human or policy intent, but it frequently demands infeasible joint accelerations or violates spatial bounding envelopes.
- **Tap 2: The mapped command ($a_{\text{cmd}}$, "Mapped"):** The kinematically retargeted setpoint (such as Cartesian end-effector velocities converted to joint space setpoints via inverse kinematics), incorporating coordinate frame transformations, trajectory interpolation, and workspace limits before transmission across the fieldbus.
- **Tap 3: The enforced command ($a_{\text{enf}}$, "Allowed"):** Logged on the bare-metal MCU on the permission side of the boundary, this represents the command after deterministic Control Barrier Functions (CBFs, @sec-enforcement-safe-sets-conditional-permission), velocity and acceleration clamps, torque saturation envelopes, and collision guards have checked or modified the proposal. For a training objective that imitates permitted commands, the loss can take the following form:
  $$\mathcal{L}_{\text{policy}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{(o_t, a_{\text{enf}, t}) \sim \mathcal{D}} \left[ \mathcal{D}_{\text{loss}}(\pi_\theta(o_t), a_{\text{enf}, t}) \right],$$
  Here the training dataset must contain curated, correctly attributed targets. Passing the permission check does not make a command an expert demonstration: a clamp or emergency stop may be a safeguard's response to a poor request. Override flags and the other taps determine which records can serve as imitation targets and which remain evidence of intervention.
- **Tap 4: The measured response ($a_{\text{meas}}$, "Done"):** The physical plant reaction measured by optical joint encoders and motor current shunt resistors over the executed control tick, recording actual mechanical displacement and electrical effort. This measured response serves as proprioceptive state input ($o_{\text{proprio}, t+1}$) for subsequent policy steps rather than an action label.

The distinction matters when the command and the motion disagree. If a teleoperator requests a rapid movement that the permission path clamps, the resulting state transition follows the enforced command. Pairing that transition only with the request hides the intervention and can teach a policy to repeat demands the machine did not execute.

At the latch, the opposite ambiguity arises. Contact resistance can bring measured joint velocities to zero ($\dot{\mathbf{q}}_{\text{meas}} \approx \mathbf{0}$) while the motors continue exerting holding torque. Treating that response as a deliberate zero-velocity target loses the distinction between maintaining effort against the latch and choosing to stop. The appropriate imitation target depends on the policy's action interface; the other taps explain how that target became physical motion.

Together the four taps form the **four-stream action tap**\index{Four-stream action tap!definition}\index{Action tap!definition} $(a_{\text{req}}, a_{\text{cmd}}, a_{\text{enf}}, a_{\text{meas}})$, one action recorded at each of its four causal stages. Keeping all four is what makes any single choice of label interpretable. A policy trained on the request alone learns commands the permission path would have clamped, and one trained on the measured response alone learns the arm's compliance, backlash, and external disturbances as if they were intended control. A log that keeps only the final encoder state or only the operator's input discards exactly the stages at which software and safety hardware changed the command. The tuple is also only as good as its shared clock. The application processor and the MCU must stamp their taps in one hardware-synchronized timebase, such as the IEEE 1588 Precision Time Protocol (PTP), written $t_{\text{PTP}}$, because a few milliseconds of skew between them misaligns each visual observation with the torque it prompted (@sec-data-multimodal-time-sync).

For the latch campaign, we choose the mapped command as the imitation target when it represents an expert request that the permission path accepted unchanged. A modified command remains a separate, attributed intervention; a curated recovery can later supply an expert target at that state. Each training pair joins the observation at its capture time to the expert command issued from the available observation history, with the command response interval recorded separately. The alignment developed below interpolates encoder state to each image's exposure midpoint; that aligns observations, but it does not move a later human decision backward in time.

### Multi-modal time synchronization and exposure midpoint alignment {#sec-data-multimodal-time-sync}

Recording the right action tap does not settle when each recorded value was physically true. In embodied platforms, sensory modalities operate at widely different sampling cadences and physical propagation regimes: cameras integrate photons over exposure windows of $10\text{--}35\text{ ms}$ at $30\text{--}60\text{ Hz}$, 6-axis force-torque sensors stream over a serial peripheral interface or a Controller Area Network (CAN) bus at $100\text{--}500\text{ Hz}$, joint and permission telemetry is retained at the MCU's chosen $1\text{ kHz}$ tick while motor-drive current sampling serves the faster local current loop, and neural policy models dispatch setpoints at $10\text{--}50\text{ Hz}$. A naive data loader that simply latches the latest available sensor sample pairs each action with a camera frame whose exposure was centered $25\text{--}40\text{ ms}$ before the frame arrived in host memory. The resulting policy learns to map historical visual states to present actions, baking artificial phase lag directly into its weights.

```{python}
#| label: calc-data-sync-displacement
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ OBSERVATION-ACTION SYNC DISPLACEMENT (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-data-multimodal-time-sync
# │ Goal:    Compare the displacement an uncompensated observation-action lag
# │          injects against the latch clearance, at transit and latch speeds.
# │ Show:    Displacement at 0.50 m/s transit and at the two latch approaches;
# │          the largest tolerable lag at each latch speed.
# │ How:     dx = v * lag; lag_max = clearance / v. Latch speeds from AISLE;
# │          transit speed, lag, and clearance are chapter-local scenario inputs.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_length, fmt_velocity, fmt_latency, fmt_multiple, check

AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class SyncDisplacement:
    """Displacement from pairing an observation with an action across a lag."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    v_transit = 0.50 * meter / second  # generic arm transit speed; category: illustrative
    t_lag = 35.0 * millisecond  # uncompensated exposure-to-arrival lag; category: illustrative
    clearance = 2.0 * millimeter  # latch clearance; scenario assumption; category: illustrative
    v_guarded = AISLE.v_latch_approach  # category: illustrative
    v_fast = AISLE.v_latch_high  # category: illustrative
    t_skew_lo = 15.0 * millisecond  # full-frame rolling-shutter skew, fast readout; category: illustrative
    t_skew_hi = 33.0 * millisecond  # full-frame rolling-shutter skew, one 30 Hz frame; category: illustrative
    clearance_tight = 1.0 * millimeter  # tighter strike plate asked about in the checkpoint; category: illustrative

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    dx_transit = (v_transit * t_lag).to(millimeter)
    dx_guarded = (v_guarded * t_lag).to(millimeter)
    dx_fast = (v_fast * t_lag).to(millimeter)
    transit_over_clearance = (dx_transit / clearance).to("").magnitude
    lag_max_guarded = (clearance / v_guarded).to(millisecond)
    lag_max_fast = (clearance / v_fast).to(millisecond)
    dx_skew_transit = (v_transit * t_skew_hi).to(millimeter)
    dx_skew_fast = (v_fast * t_skew_hi).to(millimeter)
    lag_max_tight = (clearance_tight / v_fast).to(millisecond)  # checkpoint answer; not printed

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Assertions) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(dx_transit.magnitude - 17.5) < 1e-9, "Transit displacement should be 17.5 mm")
    check(dx_guarded < clearance, "The guarded approach should fit the clearance at this lag")
    check(dx_fast > clearance, "The faster approach should exceed the clearance at this lag")
    check(abs(lag_max_fast.magnitude - 20.0) < 1e-9, "Largest tolerable lag at 0.10 m/s should be 20 ms")
    check(dx_skew_fast > clearance, "Worst-case rolling-shutter skew at 0.10 m/s should exceed the clearance")
    check(lag_max_tight < t_lag, "The checkpoint's tighter plate should reject the uncompensated lag at the faster approach")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    v_transit_str = fmt_velocity(v_transit, precision=2)
    t_lag_str = fmt_latency(t_lag, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    clearance_str = fmt_length(clearance, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    v_guarded_str = fmt_velocity(v_guarded, precision=2)
    v_fast_str = fmt_velocity(v_fast, precision=2)
    dx_transit_str = fmt_length(dx_transit, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    dx_guarded_str = fmt_length(dx_guarded, unit=millimeter, precision=2)
    dx_fast_str = fmt_length(dx_fast, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    transit_over_clearance_mult_str = fmt_multiple(transit_over_clearance, precision=1)
    lag_max_guarded_str = fmt_latency(lag_max_guarded, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    lag_max_fast_str = fmt_latency(lag_max_fast, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_skew_lo_str = fmt_latency(t_skew_lo, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_skew_hi_str = fmt_latency(t_skew_hi, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    dx_skew_transit_str = fmt_length(dx_skew_transit, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    dx_skew_fast_str = fmt_length(dx_skew_fast, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    clearance_tight_str = fmt_length(clearance_tight, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
```

To quantify the physical hazard of temporal misalignment, consider the spatial tracking error $\Delta \mathbf{x}_{\text{sync}}$ injected into the dataset when an observation and an action are paired across an uncompensated phase lag $\Delta t_{\text{lag}}$:
$$\Delta \mathbf{x}_{\text{sync}}(t) = \int_{t - \Delta t_{\text{lag}}}^t \mathbf{v}(\tau)\,d\tau \approx \mathbf{v}(t) \cdot \Delta t_{\text{lag}}.$$ {#eq-data-sync-displacement}
The latch campaign moves far more slowly than an arm in transit, and \ref{nbk-data-pairing-lag} applies @eq-data-sync-displacement at both speeds.

::: {#nbk-data-pairing-lag .callout-notebook title="The pairing lag"}

**Problem**: A logger pairs each action with a camera frame whose exposure midpoint lies an uncompensated `{python} SyncDisplacement.t_lag_str` earlier. Does the resulting pairing error fit the `{python} SyncDisplacement.clearance_str` latch clearance at transit speed and at the latch campaign's two approach speeds, and how much lag can each approach tolerate?

**Variables**:

- Uncompensated lag $\Delta t_{\text{lag}} =$ `{python} SyncDisplacement.t_lag_str` (illustrative; exposure-to-arrival delay of an untimed logger)
- Latch clearance $c =$ `{python} SyncDisplacement.clearance_str` (illustrative)
- Transit speed `{python} SyncDisplacement.v_transit_str` (illustrative); guarded approach `{python} SyncDisplacement.v_guarded_str` and faster approach `{python} SyncDisplacement.v_fast_str` (illustrative scenario speeds of the running machine)

**Math**:

1. **Transit**: `{python} SyncDisplacement.v_transit_str` $\times$ `{python} SyncDisplacement.t_lag_str` $=$ `{python} SyncDisplacement.dx_transit_str`, `{python} SyncDisplacement.transit_over_clearance_mult_str` the clearance.
2. **Guarded approach**: `{python} SyncDisplacement.v_guarded_str` $\times$ `{python} SyncDisplacement.t_lag_str` $=$ `{python} SyncDisplacement.dx_guarded_str`, inside the clearance.
3. **Faster approach**: `{python} SyncDisplacement.v_fast_str` $\times$ `{python} SyncDisplacement.t_lag_str` $=$ `{python} SyncDisplacement.dx_fast_str`, outside it.
4. **Lag ceilings**: $\Delta t_{\text{lag,max}} = c/v$, so `{python} SyncDisplacement.clearance_str` $/$ `{python} SyncDisplacement.v_guarded_str` $=$ `{python} SyncDisplacement.lag_max_guarded_str` and `{python} SyncDisplacement.clearance_str` $/$ `{python} SyncDisplacement.v_fast_str` $=$ `{python} SyncDisplacement.lag_max_fast_str`.

**Result**: The same lag is harmless at the guarded approach and disqualifying at the faster one.

**Systems insight**: A timing error becomes a position error at the speed of the motion, just as observation age becomes blind travel $v\,\tau_{\text{delay}}$ in the stopping budget. The faster approach cannot be collected without the exposure-midpoint alignment of the four-stage pipeline that follows.

:::

When an imitation learning model trains on misaligned pairs, it fits a relationship in which the action appears to precede the visual evidence that prompted it. During closed-loop deployment, that artificial phase lag appears as overshoot, control hunting, and chattering against rigid surfaces. @Fig-05-sync-displacement plots the same displacement against the lag for all three speeds.

::: {#fig-05-sync-displacement fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**One lag, three verdicts**: Pairing an observation with an action across an uncompensated lag displaces the recorded state by speed times lag. At `{python} SyncDisplacement.t_lag_str` the transit pairing is `{python} SyncDisplacement.dx_transit_str` off, the faster latch approach exceeds the `{python} SyncDisplacement.clearance_str` clearance, and the guarded approach stays inside it. The clearance tolerates at most `{python} SyncDisplacement.lag_max_fast_str` of lag at `{python} SyncDisplacement.v_fast_str` and `{python} SyncDisplacement.lag_max_guarded_str` at `{python} SyncDisplacement.v_guarded_str`; a full-frame rolling-shutter skew alone spans `{python} SyncDisplacement.t_skew_lo_str` to `{python} SyncDisplacement.t_skew_hi_str`." fig-alt="Log-log plot of pairing displacement in millimeters against observation-to-action lag in milliseconds, 1 to 100 ms. Three straight parallel lines: transit at 0.50 meters per second on top, the faster latch approach at 0.10 meters per second, and the guarded approach at 0.03 meters per second at the bottom. A red dashed horizontal line marks the 2 millimeter latch clearance. A dotted vertical line at 35 ms marks the uncompensated lag, with a dot on each line. Red squares where the latch lines cross the clearance are labeled at most 20 ms and at most 66.7 ms. A gray band from 15 to 33 ms marks full-frame rolling-shutter skew."}

```{python}
#| label: fig-05-sync-displacement
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ OBSERVATION-ACTION LAG AGAINST THE LATCH CLEARANCE (FIGURE)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-05-sync-displacement in @sec-data-multimodal-time-sync,
# │          after calc-data-sync-displacement.
# │ Goal:    Show that the same pairing lag is harmless at the guarded approach
# │          and disqualifying at the faster one.
# │ Show:    dx = v * lag for the transit and both latch speeds; the latch
# │          clearance; the 35 ms uncompensated lag; each speed's largest
# │          tolerable lag; the full-frame rolling-shutter skew band.
# │ How:     Every value reads SyncDisplacement (no literals).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from mlsysim import viz
from mlsysim.fmt import check

S = SyncDisplacement
ms = lambda q: q.to(millisecond).magnitude
mm = lambda q: q.to(millimeter).magnitude
mmps = lambda q: q.to(millimeter / millisecond).magnitude
c = mm(S.clearance)
lag = ms(S.t_lag)
lines = [  # label, speed, role color
    (f"transit {S.v_transit_str}", mmps(S.v_transit), "#4A5568"),
    (f"faster latch approach {S.v_fast_str}", mmps(S.v_fast), "#B87333"),
    (f"guarded latch approach {S.v_guarded_str}", mmps(S.v_guarded), "#007A87"),
]
check(abs(mmps(S.v_transit) * lag - mm(S.dx_transit)) < 1e-9, "transit line matches dx_transit")
check(abs(c / mmps(S.v_fast) - ms(S.lag_max_fast)) < 1e-9, "fast crossing matches lag_max_fast")

fig, ax, COLORS, plt = viz.setup_plot(figsize=(6.4, 3.4))
t = np.geomspace(1, 100, 400)
ax.axvspan(ms(S.t_skew_lo), ms(S.t_skew_hi), color="#A0AEC0", alpha=0.18, lw=0)
ax.text((ms(S.t_skew_lo) * ms(S.t_skew_hi)) ** 0.5, 60, "full-frame\nrolling-shutter skew", fontsize=7.5, color="#4A5568", ha="center", va="top")
ax.axhline(c, color="#A51C30", lw=1.2, ls=(0, (5, 3)))
ax.text(1.1, c * 1.1, f"latch clearance {S.clearance_str}", fontsize=8, color="#A51C30", ha="left", va="bottom")
ax.axvline(lag, color="#1A202C", lw=0.9, ls=(0, (2, 2)))
ax.text(lag * 1.05, 0.12, f"uncompensated\nlag {S.t_lag_str}", fontsize=7.5, color="#1A202C", va="bottom")
for lab, v, col in lines:
    ax.plot(t, v * t, color=col, lw=1.8)
    ax.plot(lag, v * lag, "o", color=col, ms=5, zorder=5)
    ax.text(105, v * 100, lab, fontsize=7.5, color=col, va="center")
for v, lab in ((mmps(S.v_fast), S.lag_max_fast_str), (mmps(S.v_guarded), S.lag_max_guarded_str)):
    tx = c / v
    ax.plot(tx, c, "s", color="#A51C30", ms=4.5, zorder=6)
    ax.text(tx * 1.07, c * 0.86, f"≤ {lab}", fontsize=7.5, color="#A51C30", ha="left", va="top")
ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_xlim(1, 100)
ax.set_ylim(0.1, 100)
ax.set_xlabel("observation-to-action pairing lag (ms)")
ax.set_ylabel("pairing displacement (mm)")
for s in ("top", "right"):
    ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
plt.close()
```
:::

#### Hardware timestamps vs. software arrival timestamps {#sec-data-hw-vs-sw-timestamps}

The root of temporal corruption lies in conflating when an optical or electrical event occurred in physics with when the operating system kernel noticed it in software:

- **Software arrival timestamps ($t_{\text{host}}$):** In naive logging pipelines, an image frame or CAN packet is timestamped when the Linux kernel handles the device interrupt or when a user-space thread dequeues the buffer from Video4Linux2 (V4L2) or a socket. This host timestamp incorporates camera pixel readout time, USB3 or MIPI CSI-2 bus serialization, Direct Memory Access (DMA) latency, and operating system scheduling jitter:
  $$t_{\text{host}} = t_{\text{mid}} + \frac{\Delta t_{\text{exp}}}{2} + t_{\text{readout}} + t_{\text{bus}} + t_{\text{driver\_irq}} + \delta_{\text{jitter}}.$$
  Host timestamps lag physical reality by $20\text{--}45\text{ ms}$. In an untuned system, operating system scheduling jitter ($\delta_{\text{jitter}} = \pm 5\text{--}15\text{ ms}$), driven by kernel preemption latency, CPU C-state power wake-up transitions, and USB host controller interrupt coalescing (where packets are held in hardware buffers until a threshold count or timer expires), corrupts numerical differentiation. When joint velocities are computed via backward difference:
  $$\dot{\mathbf{q}}_k = \frac{\mathbf{q}_k - \mathbf{q}_{k-1}}{t_k - t_{k-1}},$$
  a nominal $1\text{ kHz}$ sampling interval ($\Delta t = 1.0\text{ ms}$) perturbed by software timestamp jitter $\delta_{\text{jitter}} = \pm 0.5\text{ ms}$ causes the denominator to fluctuate between $0.5\text{ ms}$ and $1.5\text{ ms}$, doubling the inferred velocity at the shorter interval or reducing it by one third at the longer interval for the same measured displacement. If thread preemption reverses packet dequeuing order ($t_k < t_{k-1}$), the computed velocity reverses sign, injecting spurious velocity spikes into the training targets.
- **Hardware PTP timestamps ($t_{\text{PTP}}$):** Hardware timestamps remove host scheduling delay from the recorded event time. PTP estimates clock offset using a two-way exchange.[^fn-ptp-pairing-bias] The reference clock sends at $t_1$ and receives the reply at $t_4$; the remote clock receives at $t_2$ and replies at $t_3$. Under symmetric path delays, the propagation delay and offset are:
  $$\tau_{\text{prop}} = \frac{(t_4 - t_1) - (t_3 - t_2)}{2}, \qquad \theta_{\text{offset}} = \frac{(t_2 - t_1) - (t_4 - t_3)}{2}.$$
  The symmetric-path assumption matters. Hardware timestamping does not make clock conversion exact, and a network timestamp is not automatically a camera exposure timestamp. The record must retain the capture event, clock identity, and bounded conversion error. @Sec-appendix-systems-ptp develops the exchange and its uncertainty; the collection decision here is whether that uncertainty fits the task's spatial alignment tolerance.

[^fn-ptp-pairing-bias]: **Precision Time Protocol (PTP)**\index{IEEE 1588 Precision Time Protocol!pairing error}: IEEE 1588 was first published in 2002 for test-and-measurement and industrial-automation networks, and its current revision dates from 2019 [@ieee15882019]. It reaches sub-microsecond agreement only when both endpoints timestamp packets in hardware at the network interface. Its weak point is the symmetric-path assumption in the offset formula, because a link whose two directions differ in delay biases the computed offset by half that difference, and every observation-action pairing in the archive inherits the bias.

#### Rolling shutter skew across camera streams {#sec-data-rolling-shutter-skew}

A severe and frequently overlooked visual artifact in physical AI pipelines is **rolling shutter skew**. Low-cost consumer sensors and webcams expose pixel rows sequentially rather than instantaneously. For a sensor with $H$ vertical scanlines and line readout duration $\tau_{\text{line}}$, the exposure midpoint of row $y \in [0, H-1]$ depends linearly on its vertical coordinate:
$$t_{\text{row}}(y) = t_{\text{start}} + y \cdot \tau_{\text{line}} + \frac{\Delta t_{\text{exp}}}{2}.$$
Across a full frame, the temporal skew between the top row ($y = 0$) and bottom row ($y = H - 1$) accumulates to:
$$\Delta t_{\text{skew}} = (H - 1) \cdot \tau_{\text{line}},$$ {#eq-data-rolling-shutter-skew}
which for common sensors lies between about `{python} SyncDisplacement.t_skew_lo_str` and `{python} SyncDisplacement.t_skew_hi_str`, the upper end being one full frame period at 30 Hz. When the robot arm or camera moves at `{python} SyncDisplacement.v_transit_str`, the bottom of the manipulator in the image is captured while the physical link has moved up to `{python} SyncDisplacement.dx_skew_transit_str` relative to the top of the link in the same frame. Even at the faster latch approach of `{python} SyncDisplacement.v_fast_str`, the worst-case skew moves the gripper `{python} SyncDisplacement.dx_skew_fast_str` within one frame, more than the `{python} SyncDisplacement.clearance_str` clearance. This geometric warping (the "jello effect") deforms straight edges into curved arcs and breaks rigid-body geometry.

Independent rolling shutters can depict the same moving arm at different poses within nominally simultaneous frames. Hardware-triggered global shutters simplify alignment; rolling shutters require a row-time model and a motion bound or correction. Sensor choice must follow the task tolerance rather than a universal requirement for one shutter type.

A collection pipeline can implement the alignment contract in four stages:

1. **Hardware-triggered optical exposure midpoint:** The real-time MCU dispatches hardware GPIO sync pulses or PTP-synchronized trigger packets to every triggerable camera. The rig mixes shutter types: the wrist camera's global shutter exposes all rows together, while the navigation camera and the external cameras' color sensors read out row by row, so their frames also need the row-time model above to assign each row its own midpoint. The camera latches the trigger at $t_{\text{start}}$, and the driver calculates the true optical midpoint $t_{\text{mid}} = t_{\text{start}} + \Delta t_{\text{exp}} / 2$ in hardware PTP clock units ($t_{\text{PTP}}$), avoiding host arrival time as the exposure timestamp.[^fn-trigger-camera-exposure]
2. **Lock-free time-sorted jitter compensation:** Because network and bus transfers exhibit variable transport delay $\delta_{\text{jitter}}$, incoming sensor packets are stamped with their hardware PTP capture timestamp and inserted into a lock-free, time-sorted jitter ring buffer in shared memory. An asynchronous consumer thread advances a playhead lagging real-time by a fixed, bounded window ($\tau_{\text{jitter}} = 15\text{--}25\text{ ms}$), absorbing transport bursts and re-ordering packets into monotonic hardware timestamp sequence.
3. **Cubic Hermite kinematic interpolation:** Because joint encoders sample at $1\text{ kHz}$ ($1\text{ ms}$ period) while cameras capture at $30\text{ Hz}$ or $60\text{ Hz}$, the camera midpoint $t_{\text{mid}}$ falls between two discrete MCU telemetry ticks $t_k$ and $t_{k+1}$. The synchronization thread interpolates joint angles $\mathbf{q}(t_{\text{mid}})$ using cubic Hermite splines across the bounding kinematic records $(t_k, \mathbf{q}_k, \dot{\mathbf{q}}_k)$ and $(t_{k+1}, \mathbf{q}_{k+1}, \dot{\mathbf{q}}_{k+1})$:
   $$\mathbf{q}(t_{\text{mid}}) = h_{00}(\lambda) \mathbf{q}_k + h_{10}(\lambda) \Delta t_s \dot{\mathbf{q}}_k + h_{01}(\lambda) \mathbf{q}_{k+1} + h_{11}(\lambda) \Delta t_s \dot{\mathbf{q}}_{k+1},$$
   where $\Delta t_s = t_{k+1} - t_k = 1\text{ ms}$, $\lambda = (t_{\text{mid}} - t_k)/\Delta t_s \in [0, 1]$ is the fraction of the tick elapsed at the exposure midpoint, and $h_{ij}(\lambda)$ are the cubic Hermite basis functions (@sec-appendix-control-splines). This gives a smooth state estimate between valid samples. The interpolation error still needs a bound, especially across contact or missing telemetry.
4. **Pre-serialization alignment:** Container formats store multi-rate topics with the timestamps provided by the logger. Alignment may occur during capture or in a versioned preprocessing pass. Preserve the raw timestamps and interpolation provenance in either case, so the training pair carries an estimated state and its uncertainty rather than an assertion of exact simultaneity.

The same pairing contract governs deployment. A policy trained on aligned pairs must also be fed aligned observations and have its actions executed when the training data implies. UMI measures each observation stream's latency and aligns all streams to the slowest, usually the camera, then sends commands ahead of time to cover the arm's and gripper's execution latency and discards actions whose execution time has already passed; with latency matching disabled, the same policy's motion became visibly jittery [@chi2024umi]. UMI also expresses actions relative to the gripper's current pose rather than in a fixed robot frame, which removes the dependence on a base calibration and lets one policy run on more than one arm.

[^fn-trigger-camera-exposure]: **Hardware Exposure Triggering**\index{Camera triggering!hardware sync pulse}: A dedicated GPIO or TTL pulse from the real-time microcontroller starts every camera's exposure on the same electrical edge, instead of a software trigger issued through the host's driver stack. Triggered global-shutter cameras then begin exposing within microseconds of one another, which leaves the exposure duration, not the trigger path, as the dominant term in the midpoint timestamp.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The capture timestamp, taken in hardware at the exposure midpoint, is defined for every sensor in @sec-perception-handoff.
:::

::: {#chk-data-action-label-timing .callout-checkpoint title="Action labels and pairing time"}

A training pair is only as trustworthy as the tap it imitates and the time it assigns to each observation.

- [ ] **Clamped request**: A teleoperator requests a motion that the permission path clamps. Which tap does the resulting state transition follow, and where does the record keep the evidence of the clamp?
- [ ] **Stalled latch**: Measured joint velocity is zero while the motors hold torque against the latch. Why is $a_{\text{meas}}$ the wrong imitation target at that step?
- [ ] **Unchanged mapped command**: Under what condition can $a_{\text{cmd}}$ serve as the expert target, and what happens to the pair when that condition fails?
- [ ] **Lag budget**: A tighter strike plate leaves only `{python} SyncDisplacement.clearance_tight_str` of clearance. At the faster approach of `{python} SyncDisplacement.v_fast_str`, what is the largest uncompensated lag the pairing tolerates, and does a logger with the `{python} SyncDisplacement.t_lag_str` lag of \ref{nbk-data-pairing-lag} meet it?

:::

A tap and a timestamp are only as good as the loop that produced them. In teleoperation that loop runs through a human, and the interface between human and machine shapes the recorded dynamics long before the data reaches a model.

## Teleoperation Demonstration Costs {#sec-data-teleop-costs}

Teleoperation remains the standard way to gather high-quality physical trajectories, and in physical data engineering it is best understood as an asynchronous data-generation pipeline with a human inside its control loop (@fig-05-teleop-rig). A workspace camera captures the physical scene and streams encoded frames across a network fabric to an operator console; the human operator perceives the visual display, cognitively decides on a trajectory correction, and displaces an input device; the host workstation maps that motion into a kinematically retargeted setpoint and transmits it across a fieldbus to the motor drives; the actuators accelerate the robot's physical links against inertia, friction, and environmental contact; and the updated scene arrives at the camera sensor on the subsequent cycle.

::: {#fig-05-teleop-rig fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Kinematically isomorphic teleoperation loop**: The operator moves a leader arm whose joints mirror the follower's, and the host copies joint angles across, as in low-cost leader-follower rigs such as GELLO [@wu2023gello]. Because the leader shares the follower's joint structure, the interface needs no inverse kinematics and inherits none of its singularities (configurations where joints align and the arm loses a direction of motion), preserving the operator's direct joint-level coordination. The loop still closes through the operator: human reaction, command transfer, mechanical response, and display delay all enter the recording as phase lag, so the demonstration carries the operator's delay as if it were policy." fig-alt="Block diagram of a teleoperation loop. An operator box labeled see, decide, move sends an arrow labeled t hum to a small leader arm with joints q1, q2, and q3. The leader feeds a joint copy box stating q follower equals q leader, noted no inverse kinematics, which sends an arrow labeled t cmd to a larger follower arm with the same three joints, reaching toward a latch across a gap labeled t mech. A dashed arrow runs from the follower down to a workspace camera, whose arrow labeled t disp runs left to a display, which feeds back up to the operator."}
![](images/svg/fig05_leader_follower_loop.svg){width="100%"}
:::

The rig in @fig-05-teleop-rig maps each leader joint directly to the corresponding follower joint ($\mathbf{q}_{\text{leader}} \equiv \mathbf{q}_{\text{follower}}$), avoiding numerical inverse kinematics in the input mapping. The demonstration still carries the operator's visual-neuromuscular response and the transport delay, whose combined effect limits corrective timing.

### Human-in-the-loop latency and bilateral passivity breakdown {#sec-data-bilateral-passivity}

```{python}
#| label: calc-data-teleop-loop-latency
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ TELEOPERATION ROUND-TRIP LATENCY (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-data-bilateral-passivity
# │ Goal:    Sum the four stages of the human-in-the-loop correction and show
# │          that the operator's own reaction dominates the loop.
# │ Show:    Display, human, command, and mechanical latencies; their sum; the
# │          instant the correction is commanded; the human share.
# │ How:     t_loop = t_disp + t_hum + t_cmd + t_mech. Stage values are the
# │          chapter's illustrative reference setup (see the Reader Guide).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_latency, fmt_percent, check

class TeleopLoopLatency:
    """Round-trip latency of one teleoperated correction."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    t_disp = 50.0 * millisecond  # exposure, decode, raster refresh; category: illustrative
    t_hum = 200.0 * millisecond  # perception, planning, neuromuscular; category: illustrative
    t_cmd = 10.0 * millisecond  # quantization, packetization, bus; category: illustrative
    t_mech = 80.0 * millisecond  # torque ramp and structural inertia; category: illustrative

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    t_loop = (t_disp + t_hum + t_cmd + t_mech).to(millisecond)
    t_commanded = (t_disp + t_hum).to(millisecond)  # correction commanded after contact
    hum_share = (t_hum / t_loop).to("").magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Assertions) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    # margin_teleop_loop_latency_strip.svg fig-alt hand-types the same stage values.
    check(abs(t_loop.magnitude - 340.0) < 1e-9, "Round-trip latency should be 340 ms")
    check(abs(t_commanded.magnitude - 250.0) < 1e-9, "Correction should be commanded 250 ms after contact")
    check(t_hum > t_disp + t_cmd + t_mech, "The operator's reaction should exceed the other stages combined")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    t_disp_str = fmt_latency(t_disp, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_hum_str = fmt_latency(t_hum, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_cmd_str = fmt_latency(t_cmd, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_mech_str = fmt_latency(t_mech, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_loop_str = fmt_latency(t_loop, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_commanded_str = fmt_latency(t_commanded, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    hum_share_str = fmt_percent(hum_share, precision=1)
```

Each stage in this distributed loop introduces latency that affects the timing of the correction. In a reference setup with a high-speed camera and a wired local network (illustrative; see the Reader Guide), display processing requires $t_{\text{disp}} =$ `{python} TeleopLoopLatency.t_disp_str` across exposure integration, H.264 decoding, and monitor raster refresh. Human visual perception, cognitive motor planning, and neuromuscular transmission introduce an operator response latency of $t_{\text{hum}} =$ `{python} TeleopLoopLatency.t_hum_str` for continuous path corrections. Command quantization, packetization, and bus transport to the robot controller add $t_{\text{cmd}} =$ `{python} TeleopLoopLatency.t_cmd_str`. Actuator torque ramp-up and structural inertia impose a mechanical response latency of $t_{\text{mech}} =$ `{python} TeleopLoopLatency.t_mech_str` before the robot achieves the commanded acceleration. The **teleoperation round-trip latency** $t_{\text{loop}}$, the time from a contact event to the corrective actuator response, is their sum:
$$t_{\text{loop}} = t_{\text{disp}} + t_{\text{hum}} + t_{\text{cmd}} + t_{\text{mech}}.$$ {#eq-data-teleop-loop-latency}

When a contact misalignment occurs at time $t$, the operator sees it on the display `{python} TeleopLoopLatency.t_disp_str` later, commands a physical correction `{python} TeleopLoopLatency.t_commanded_str` after the event, and the arm pushes back after `{python} TeleopLoopLatency.t_loop_str`, while the arm keeps moving under momentum and contact forces. A logger that naively pairs the observation $s_t$ with the command issued at the same instant pairs a state with an action chosen for a state `{python} TeleopLoopLatency.t_commanded_str` older. The policy learns that delay as deliberate behavior and over-corrects or oscillates when it runs autonomously at the control rate. The round-trip latency is therefore a property of the dataset, not only of the rig, because it enters every demonstration as phase lag dominated by the operator's own reaction time, `{python} TeleopLoopLatency.hum_share_str` percent of the loop in this setup.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_teleop_loop_latency_strip.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="One horizontal bar divided into the four stages of a teleoperated correction, drawn to scale under a bracket labeled 340 milliseconds loop: display 50 ms, human 200 ms, command 10 ms, and mechanics 80 ms. The human segment is the longest by far."}

*The operator's own reaction is `{python} TeleopLoopLatency.hum_share_str` percent of the `{python} TeleopLoopLatency.t_loop_str` correction loop.*
:::

Force reflection adds another constraint to the collection interface. In **bilateral teleoperation**, the operator moves the leader while the follower's contact force returns through a delayed link. The work delivered at that port over a cycle is:
$$\Delta E = \int_0^{T_{\text{cycle}}} F_{\text{contact}}(t - \tau) v(t)\,dt.$$
The sign depends on the force–velocity phase relationship; delay does not make every interaction unstable. It can compromise the passivity[^fn-passivity-delay-teleop] of the coupled system and excite oscillation [@anderson1989bilateral]. Wave variables or passivity controllers address that risk under their stated assumptions (@sec-appendix-control-passivity). For collection, the consequence is a label-fidelity trade-off: filtering that stabilizes force feedback can also attenuate the contact transients the operator needs to demonstrate. Record the feedback and filtering configuration alongside the trajectory.
